1. Core Clinical Tension: A 19-year-old man in the Brazilian Amazon admitted with acute abdominal pain and hemoperitoneum resulting from splenic rupture after jumping from a tree without direct abdominal impact. Emergency splenectomy reveals massive pathological splenomegaly (1,300 g) with capsular tearing. Postoperatively, he develops severe high fever, rigors, myalgias, anemia (Hb 8.7 g/dL), and severe thrombocytopenia (66,000/mm³). The clinical tension centers on recognizing that the acute surgical event was actually a catastrophic complication (pathological splenic rupture) of an acute tropical parasitic infection contracted during rural construction work, rather than an isolated traumatic tear or postoperative bacterial sepsis.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The case prompt encompasses his urban residence in Manaus, rural construction work in an endemic Amazonian zone over the preceding month, prodromal feverish sensation, headache, and asthenia for 2 days prior to presentation, acute abdominal pain after jumping from a tree without direct trauma, emergent splenectomy findings (massive 1,300 g spleen with colic surface capsular rupture and intra-abdominal hemorrhage), and postoperative presentation with high fever, chills, generalized myalgias, hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, and platelets 66,000/mm³. The breakpoint is set immediately prior to transfer to the tertiary infectious disease hospital, peripheral thick blood smear examination, and PCR.
3. Differential Distinctions: Isolated traumatic splenic rupture cannot explain the massive 1,300 g organ weight (normal adult spleen ~150 g) in the absence of direct blunt abdominal impact, nor does it explain antecedent febrile prodrome and marked post-op bicytopenia. Severe postoperative bacterial sepsis / bacteremia can manifest with high fever, rigors, and thrombocytopenia, but blood smears and lack of purulent focus point directly to intraerythrocytic protozoan parasitemia. Mononucleosis (EBV) or visceral leishmaniasis can cause splenomegaly, but acute cyclic high fever and high-grade thrombocytopenia in the Amazonian basin strongly implicate Plasmodium infection.
case_prompt:
A 19-year-old man residing in urban Manaus is admitted to a secondary-care hospital in the Brazilian Amazon with acute abdominal pain after jumping from a tree; he denies sustaining any direct blunt trauma to the abdomen. For the preceding month, he had been working on a construction project in an endemic rural rainforest region. He reports that for two days prior to the incident, he had been feeling feverish and experiencing mild headache and asthenia.

Evaluation revealed hemoperitoneum and splenic rupture, prompting an emergency laparotomy and splenectomy. Intraoperatively, the surgical team extracted a massively enlarged spleen weighing 1,300 grams, with a capsular tear on the colic surface.

Following surgery, the patient develops high fevers, rigors, chills, and generalized myalgias. Diagnostic laboratory evaluation performed by the surgical service reveals anemia with a hemoglobin level of 8.7 g/dL and thrombocytopenia with a platelet count of 66,000/mm³.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered initially due to the temporal onset of acute abdominal pain after jumping from a tree; however, the patient experienced no direct abdominal impact, and surgical pathology revealed a massive underlying 1,300 g spleen with prodromal constitutional symptoms, indicating pathological rather than mechanical rupture.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: acute abdominal pain after jumping from a tree denying to have suffered any direct abdominal trauma. A diagnosis of spleen rupture and intra-abdominal haemorrhage was performed. He was submitted to splenectomy, during which a large spleen of 1,300 grams with a capsule rupture in the colic surface was obtained.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered when the patient spiked high fevers with rigors and myalgias following splenectomy, but acute profound thrombocytopenia (66,000/mm³) and antecedent rural forest exposure raised high suspicion for an endemic hemoparasitic infection.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: After surgery, he developed high fever, chills, and generalized myalgia. The initial diagnostic investigation performed by the Surgery Department only revealed anemia (Hb 8.7 g/dL) and thrombocytopenia (66,000 platelets/mm3).

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Microscopic evaluation of a peripheral thick blood smear demonstrated high-grade intraerythrocytic parasitemia (10,000 to 100,000 parasites/mm³) confirmed as Plasmodium vivax monoinfection by real-time PCR, proving that acute malaria infection precipitated massive splenomegaly and subsequent capsular rupture.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: A thick blood smear disclosed P. vivax infection with a semiquantitative parasitemia between 10.000 and 100.000 parasites/mm3. Real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) from the peripheral blood confirmed P. vivax monoinfection.

editor_comments: Standardized admission diagnostic case for pathological splenic rupture secondary to Plasmodium vivax malaria. Admission breakpoint set following postoperative surgical workup and prior to peripheral blood parasitological smear/PCR.
